To: Archive project team
From: Isabel Moreno, Records Manager
Subject: Creating a searchable archive

The scanned pages in our historical collection are now online. This month's task is to prepare a short index so that employees can find relevant pages without opening every image. Each entry should include a document date, a subject phrase, and a page reference. An index entry is a search aid, not a replacement for the original page.

Use the date printed on the document, not the date of scanning. If an original has no date, enter “Undated”; do not estimate a year from surrounding files. The subject phrase should describe the content in present-day language, even when an old department name appears in the image. Retain the image exactly as scanned, including spelling mistakes and handwritten notes. If a name in the image could confuse readers, explain it briefly in the index.

The first ten entries from each team member will be checked by another member before the rest are prepared. This sample check is intended to reveal differences in how we apply the instructions. It is not a request to check the historical accuracy of the documents themselves.

Subject: Questions from the first sample

There is also a 1988 memo headed “Dispatch Pool.” That department is now called Transport Services. Nadia kept the old name as the subject phrase and suggested replacing it in the scanned image as well. I think readers should be able to see the original wording, but an explanation would help them find the memo.

Once these issues are resolved, I can give Nadia feedback. She has not begun her remaining entries, and the other team members are still preparing their samples.

Repeat only the test in room 206
Pair the pad to R208 and test emergency and timed wake-up alerts in her room

documents.title: Room Alerts for Guests
documents.text:
Room Alerts for Guests

Guests who cannot rely on an audible alarm may request a flashing receiver and a vibrating bed pad. The pad receives its signal from the room receiver, not directly from the telephone. Staff must pair the pad with the receiver’s room code and test it from that receiver before leaving the equipment with a guest. Handing over a pad does not establish that it is working in that room.

Emergency alerts and requested wake-up alerts are different functions. An emergency-system test checks the alarm signal; a scheduled wake-up test checks the separate timer. Confirm both functions if a guest requests both. A normal telephone wake-up call does not test either the flashing receiver or the pad.

Record the code and test results on the room log. If a function has not been tested, describe it as unverified rather than recording a pass.
